1.pericope_label: Leviathan slain: the sword of the Lord on the dragon in the sea

schools.summary: Identify the monsters and the sword by their sources: three epithets for three empires, drawn as animal forms, with the dragon as Egypt's standing emblem and the two serpents matched to the Tigris and the Euphrates and to the policies those rivers symbolise.

Take the verse as the whole of Satan's kingdom under one figure, destroyed by the sword of God alone, while noting that it concerns his agents rather than his person, and that the war continues until that day.

Weigh the zoology and decline the identification: the names cover crocodile, dragon and sea monster, or else one enemy under three descriptions, standing allegorically for great persecuting powers that the notes need not name.
Distribute the images among the church's historic oppressors, one always more formidable than the rest, and carry the execution forward to Christ's victory over the power of death.

positions.view: three named empires, Egypt with Assyria and Babylon, each marked by its own epithet
great potentates and persecutors in general, which particular ones being a question of great difficulty best left open
Satan and the whole of his kingdom, allegorically, though the verse touches his instruments rather than himself
every proud oppressing tyrant, and in the gospel application the devil who had the power of death

debates.question: Do the three names describe three creatures or one?

positions.view: three: the crocodile rigid along the backbone, the winding dragon, and the sea monster or whale
one enemy under three descriptions, the epithets marking its sting and its craft
one word serving for two of them, distinguished only by their adjectives

outliers.reading: Alone turns the verse into a sailing figure for the Christian life: we have continually to do with Satan as with a wild beast, and the world is the sea we sail, where such beasts work to upset the ship, so that the war is not over and an enemy vanquished a hundred times keeps renewing it.

themes: In that day the Lord with his sore and great and strong sword shall punish leviathan the piercing serpent, even leviathan that crooked serpent; and he shall slay the dragon that is in the sea.

2.pericope_label: The vineyard of red wine: no fury, and Jacob taking root

schools.summary: Read the song against the earlier song of the vineyard, clause reversing clause, and settle the wording by the versions: the wine fiery or foaming, the coming ones a future striking of root, and the whole ending as the psalm of the church to come.

Trace every part of the vineyard's worth to undeserved favour continued without a break, supply the silent interval when God seemed to have abandoned it, and hear in the last verse a promise to a church reduced to a very small number.
Recover the song's antiphonal form and assign its speaking parts, weigh the manuscripts behind wall and wrath, and read the red wine as the best wine of that country.
Set the gospel church deeper and wider than the older one, and turn the vineyard's keeping and watering into the church's continual dependence.

debates.question: How should the fourth verse open?

positions.view: Fury is not in me, God disclaiming wrath against his vineyard
I have no wall, the vineyard complaining, one letter apart from the received text and supported by the older song where the wall was taken away
yes, a responsive song with parts assigned to Jehovah and to the vineyard in turn, after the ancient manner of many nations
no, the prophet simply reappears as the hymn writer of the coming day
the church sings it in alternating response, though one reading turns the imperative into a challenge flung at her enemies

debates.question: What does the vineyard of red wine mean?

positions.view: red because the redder the wine the more it was valued
red standing in Scripture for excellence generally
the word meaning fiery or foaming, with the Greek apparently reading a beloved vineyard instead

outliers.reading: Alone supports the antiphonal reading from his own experience, reporting that he has often heard responsive singing practised at funerals among the descendants of the aboriginal Irish, and that the poems of Ossian are of that kind.

themes: In that day sing ye unto her, A vineyard of red wine.
I the Lord do keep it; I will water it every moment: lest any hurt it, I will keep it night and day.
Fury is not in me: who would set the briers and thorns against me in battle? I would go through them, I would burn them together.
Or let him take hold of my strength, that he may make peace with me; and he shall make peace with me.
He shall cause them that come of Jacob to take root: Israel shall blossom and bud, and fill the face of the world with fruit.

7.pericope_label: Chastisement in measure, and the purging of Jacob's iniquity

schools.summary: Fix the pronouns and the vocabulary before the doctrine: the comparison admits two readings, the measure is a small definite one, the putting away is a divorce plea, and the rough wind sifts rather than stays.

Read the moderation as proof of election: God gives his anger loose rein against the reprobate and restrains it towards his own, cutting branches and trunk but never the root, and chastising to prepare for a repentance that is not itself a satisfaction.

State the contrast plainly and keep to the vine: the enemies were utterly destroyed and the people were not, the luxuriant branches are cut but the stock is spared, and the altars in view may be one an actual king had built.
Note that judgment begins at the house of God, and that those he has known above all the families of the earth are punished first.

debates.question: What is the comparison in the seventh verse?

positions.view: God has not struck his own people as he struck those who struck them, whose strokes were final
God has not struck Israel as her oppressors struck her, ruthlessly and in hate, but remembered mercy in his wrath

debates.question: What is meant by debating with it when it shooteth forth?

positions.view: God contends with the affliction itself, checking it and refusing to let it pass its bounds
the vine's shoots are cut back without the stock being destroyed, the stroke reaching branch and trunk but never the root
when thou didst put her away, thou didst plead with her, a divorce plea never pressed to the limit the law allowed

debates.question: Does God stay the rough wind or sift with it?

positions.view: he stays it, mitigating the severity of the judgment
the word means sifting, not staying: he sifts with a violent breath in the day of the east wind, so that punishment following punishment is reformatory and not merely penal

outliers.reading: Alone turns the purging of iniquity into a controversy over satisfactions, putting the objection in its hardest form, that if punishment expiates then satisfactions must replace it where punishment is absent, and answering that chastisements expiate indirectly only, as remedies preparing for the repentance that obtains pardon.

themes: Hath he smitten him, as he smote those that smote him? or is he slain according to the slaughter of them that are slain by him?
In measure, when it shooteth forth, thou wilt debate with it: he stayeth his rough wind in the day of the east wind.

By this therefore shall the iniquity of Jacob be purged; and this is all the fruit to take away his sin; when he maketh all the stones of the altar as chalkstones that are beaten in sunder, the groves and images shall not stand up.

10.pericope_label: The defenced city desolate, the beating out, and the great trumpet

schools.summary: Decide the referent by the vocabulary and the sequence: the same phrase stood earlier for the enemy's city, the people without understanding may be either Israel or the world-power, the beating is of olives rather than corn, and the stream of Egypt is a border wadi and not the Nile.

Take the desolation as Jerusalem's, written to keep the godly from losing heart, and the gathering as a threshing that finds grain buried under chaff and brings it home one after another, from Chaldea and from the Egypt they had fled to against command.

Keep the vineyard figure and the local detail: withered vine twigs gathered for fuel because wood is scarce, women gathering because the men are dead, and the trumpet a summons like the one that moved the camp.

debates.question: Which is the defenced city left desolate?

positions.view: Jerusalem, and the other fortified towns with it, the prophet speaking from within the captivity
not Jerusalem, nor Samaria, nor literal Babylon, but the mystical Babylon and the whole antichristian jurisdiction
the city of the strangers, the enemy of God's people, since reading Jerusalem here breaks the sequence of thought

debates.question: What withers and is broken off?

positions.view: the boughs of the vineyard, gathered as fuel because wood is scarce in the east
shrubs grown over the open spaces of the ruined city, gathered by women without fear of trespass
the harvest, the ambiguous word meaning corn as readily as bough, cut down before it ripens

debates.question: What is the beating out in the twelfth verse?

positions.view: the threshing of corn, the people found like grain buried under chaff and gathered one after another
the beating down of olives, a full harvest set against an earlier gleaning of a few from the topmost boughs, with each single olive cared for

outliers.reading: Alone brings the chapter into his own century, expecting the prophecies of Egypt's conversion to be fulfilled once the Ottoman yoke is thrown off, and calling the Mohammedan power a genuine antichrist which the Lord will remove in due time; he alone also takes the channel of the river for the river Sabbation, on Kimchi's authority.

themes: Yet the defenced city shall be desolate, and the habitation forsaken, and left like a wilderness: there shall the calf feed, and there shall he lie down, and consume the branches thereof.

When the boughs thereof are withered, they shall be broken off: the women come, and set them on fire: for it is a people of no understanding: therefore he that made them will not have mercy on them, and he that formed them will shew them no favour.
And it shall come to pass in that day, that the Lord shall beat off from the channel of the river unto the stream of Egypt, and ye shall be gathered one by one, O ye children of Israel.

And it shall come to pass in that day, that the great trumpet shall be blown, and they shall come which were ready to perish in the land of Assyria, and the outcasts in the land of Egypt, and shall worship the Lord in the holy mount at Jerusalem.
